nodes.name: Standing hypothesis: $q$ is an even power of a prime
nodes.statement: Throughout this paper, except Section~3, $q$ is an even power of a prime number $p$.

nodes.name: Hermitian variety over ${\Bbb F}_q$ (and Hermitian polynomial)
nodes.statement: A Hermitian variety over ${\Bbb F}_q$ is a hypersurface in ${\Bbb P^n}$ defined by \begin{equation} (X_0^{\sqrt{q}}, \dots , X_n^{\sqrt{q}}) A \, {}^t\!(X_0, \dots , X_n) =0, \end{equation} where $A$ is a square matrix of order $n+1$ whose entries are in ${\Bbb F}_q$ with the property ${}^t\!A=A^{(\sqrt{q})}$; here $A^{(\sqrt{q})}$ means taking entry-wise the $\sqrt{q}$-th power, and ${}^t\!A$ is the transposed matrix of $A$. We refer this kind of polynomial as a Hermitian polynomial over ${\Bbb F}_q$.
nodes.statement_short: A hypersurface of ${\Bbb P}^n$ cut out by $(X_0^{\sqrt q},\dots)A\,{}^t(X_0,\dots)=0$ with ${}^tA = A^{(\sqrt q)}$.
differentia: $A$ is a square matrix of order $n+1$ whose entries are in ${\Bbb F}_q$ with the property ${}^t\!A=A^{(\sqrt{q})}$

nodes.name: Hermitian criterion for a form of degree $\sqrt{q}+1$
nodes.statement: For a homogeneous polynomial $F$ of degree $\sqrt{q}+1$ whose coefficients are in ${\Bbb F}_q$, the hypersurface given by $F=0$ is Hermitian if and only if there is an element $\rho \in {\Bbb F}_q^{\ast}$ such that $\rho F$ is a Hermitian polynomial.
nodes.statement_short: $\{F=0\}$ of degree $\sqrt q+1$ is Hermitian exactly when some scalar multiple $\rho F$ is a Hermitian polynomial.
assumptions: For a homogeneous polynomial $F$ of degree $\sqrt{q}+1$ whose coefficients are in ${\Bbb F}_q$
conclusions: the hypersurface given by $F=0$ is Hermitian if and only if there is an element $\rho \in {\Bbb F}_q^{\ast}$ such that $\rho F$ is a Hermitian polynomial

nodes.name: Hermitian polynomials form an ${\Bbb F}_{\!\sqrt{q}}$ vector space
nodes.statement: The family of Hermitian polynomials over ${\Bbb F}_q$ forms an ${\Bbb F}_{\! \sqrt{q}}$ vector space.
conclusions: The family of Hermitian polynomials over ${\Bbb F}_q$ forms an ${\Bbb F}_{\! \sqrt{q}}$ vector space.

nodes.name: Nonsingularity of a Hermitian variety iff $\det A \neq 0$
nodes.statement: It is obvious that the Hermitian polynomial (\ref{def_hermitian}) defines a nonsingular Hermitian variety if and only if $\det A \neq 0$.
assumptions: the Hermitian polynomial (\ref{def_hermitian})
conclusions: defines a nonsingular Hermitian variety if and only if $\det A \neq 0$

nodes.name: Standard form $H_{n-1}$ of a nonsingular Hermitian variety
nodes.statement: By the standard argument, a nonsingular Hermitian variety is projectively equivalent to the variety \begin{equation} H_{n-1} : X_0^{\sqrt{q}+1} + X_1^{\sqrt{q}+1} + \dots + X_n^{\sqrt{q}+1} =0 \end{equation} over ${\Bbb F}_q$.
nodes.statement_short: Every nonsingular Hermitian variety is projectively equivalent over ${\Bbb F}_q$ to the Fermat-type model $H_{n-1}$.
assumptions: a nonsingular Hermitian variety
conclusions: is projectively equivalent to the variety \begin{equation} H_{n-1} : X_0^{\sqrt{q}+1} + X_1^{\sqrt{q}+1} + \dots + X_n^{\sqrt{q}+1} =0 \end{equation} over ${\Bbb F}_q$.

nodes.name: Number of ${\Bbb F}_q$-points of $H_{n-1}$ (Bose-Chakravarti)
nodes.statement: The number $N_q(H_{n-1})$ of ${\Bbb F}_q$-points of $H_{n-1}$ is \begin{equation} N_q(H_{n-1}) = (\sqrt{q}^{n+1} + (-1)^{n})(\sqrt{q}^{n} + (-1)^{n-1})/(q-1), \end{equation} which is due to \cite{bos-cha1966}.
nodes.statement_short: Closed formula for the point count of the nonsingular Hermitian variety $H_{n-1}$ over ${\Bbb F}_q$.
assumptions: The number $N_q(H_{n-1})$ of ${\Bbb F}_q$-points of $H_{n-1}$

nodes.name: Weil-Deligne bound
nodes.statement: The Weil conjecture \cite{wei1949} established by Deligne \cite{del1973} implies that the number $N$ of ${\Bbb F}_q$-points of a nonsingular hypersurface of degree $d$ in ${\Bbb P}^n$ defined over ${\Bbb F}_q$ is bounded by \begin{equation} N \leq \frac{q^n -1}{q-1} + \frac{d-1}{d} \left( (d-1)^n - (-1)^n \right) \sqrt{q}^{n-1}. \end{equation} Furthermore, if equality holds in (\ref{weil_deligne}) for a certain nonsingular hypersurface of degree $d$, then $d \leq \sqrt{q}+1$.
nodes.statement_short: Deligne's proof of the Weil conjecture bounds $N$ for a nonsingular degree-$d$ hypersurface, and equality forces $d \leq \sqrt q+1$.
assumptions: the number $N$ of ${\Bbb F}_q$-points of a nonsingular hypersurface of degree $d$ in ${\Bbb P}^n$ defined over ${\Bbb F}_q$
conclusions: N \leq \frac{q^n -1}{q-1} + \frac{d-1}{d} \left( (d-1)^n - (-1)^n \right) \sqrt{q}^{n-1}.
if equality holds in (\ref{weil_deligne}) for a certain nonsingular hypersurface of degree $d$, then $d \leq \sqrt{q}+1$
nodes.origin_citation: Weil 1949; Deligne 1973 (additional claim: Sorensen 1994 Cor. 2.2, Homma & Kim 2013 Cor. 4.3)

nodes.name: $N_q(H_{n-1})$ attains the Weil-Deligne bound for $d=\sqrt{q}+1$
nodes.statement: The number $N_q(H_{n-1})$ achieves the equality in (\ref{weil_deligne}) for $d=\sqrt{q} +1$.
assumptions: for $d=\sqrt{q} +1$
conclusions: The number $N_q(H_{n-1})$ achieves the equality in (\ref{weil_deligne})

nodes.name: Hirschfeld-Storme-Thas-Voloch characterization of the Hermitian curve
nodes.statement: Suppose that $q \neq 4$. Let $C$ be a plane curve over ${\Bbb F}_q$ of degree $\sqrt{q} +1$ without ${\Bbb F}_q$-line components. If $C$ has $\sqrt{q}^3 +1$ points over ${\Bbb F}_q$, then $C$ is a Hermitian curve.
nodes.statement_short: For $q \neq 4$, a plane curve of degree $\sqrt q+1$ with no ${\Bbb F}_q$-line component and $\sqrt q^3+1$ points must be Hermitian.
assumptions: Suppose that $q \neq 4$.
Let $C$ be a plane curve over ${\Bbb F}_q$ of degree $\sqrt{q} +1$ without ${\Bbb F}_q$-line components.
If $C$ has $\sqrt{q}^3 +1$ points over ${\Bbb F}_q$
conclusions: then $C$ is a Hermitian curve

nodes.name: Main Theorem: characterization of the nonsingular Hermitian surface
nodes.statement: Let $S$ be a surface in ${\Bbb P}^3$ defined over ${\Bbb F}_q$ without ${\Bbb F}_q$-plane components. If the degree of $S$ is $\sqrt{q}+1$ and $N_q(S) = (\sqrt{q}^3+1)(q+1)$, then $S$ is a nonsingular Hermitian surface over ${\Bbb F}_q$.
nodes.statement_short: A degree-$(\sqrt q+1)$ surface in ${\Bbb P}^3$ with no ${\Bbb F}_q$-plane component and $(\sqrt q^3+1)(q+1)$ points is the nonsingular Hermitian surface.
assumptions: Let $S$ be a surface in ${\Bbb P}^3$ defined over ${\Bbb F}_q$ without ${\Bbb F}_q$-plane components.
If the degree of $S$ is $\sqrt{q}+1$ and $N_q(S) = (\sqrt{q}^3+1)(q+1)$
conclusions: then $S$ is a nonsingular Hermitian surface over ${\Bbb F}_q$

nodes.name: Notation (rational points, intersection multiplicity, tangent line)
nodes.statement: \begin{itemize} \item When $X$ is an algebraic set in ${\Bbb P}^n$ defined by equations over ${\Bbb F}_q$, the set of ${\Bbb F}_q$-points in $X$ is denoted by $X({\Bbb F}_q)$, and the cardinality of $X({\Bbb F}_q)$ by $N_q(X)$. \item When coordinates $X_0, \dots , X_n$ of ${\Bbb P}^n$ are given, for a homogeneous polynomial $h$ in those variables, $\{ h=0 \}$ means the hypersurface defined by $h=0$. \item Let $D$ and $E$ are curves in ${\Bbb P}^2$ without common components. For a point $Q \in D\cap E$, $i(D.E;Q)$ denotes the local intersection multiplicity of $D$ and $E$ at $Q$, and $(D.E) = \sum_{Q \in D \cap E} i(D.E;Q)$. \item For a plane curve $C \subset {\Bbb P}^2$ and a nonsingular point $P \in C$, $T_P(C)$ denotes the embedded tangent line to $C$ at $P$. \item The multiplicative set ${\Bbb F}_q \setminus \{0\}$ is denoted by ${\Bbb F}_q^{\ast}$. \item For a finite set $Y$, ${}^{\#}Y$ denotes the number of elements of $Y$. \end{itemize}
nodes.statement_short: Notation: $X({\Bbb F}_q)$ and $N_q(X)$ for rational points and their number, $i(D.E;Q)$ and $(D.E)$ for intersection multiplicities, $T_P(C)$ for the tangent line, ${\Bbb F}_q^{\ast}$, and ${}^{\#}Y$.

nodes.name: Sziklai bound
nodes.statement: Let $d$ be an integer with $2 \leq d \leq q+2$, and $C$ a curve of degree $d$ in ${\Bbb P}^2$ defined over ${\Bbb F}_q$ without ${\Bbb F}_q$-linear components. Then \begin{equation} N_q(C) \leq (d-1)q+1 \end{equation} except for curves over ${\Bbb F}_4$ which are projectively equivalent to the curve defined by \[ K: \ (X_0 + X_1 + X_2)^4 + (X_0X_1 + X_1X_2 +X_2X_0)^2 +X_0X_1X_2(X_0 + X_1 + X_2) =0. \] For the exceptional curve $K$ above, $N_4(K)=14$.
nodes.statement_short: A degree-$d$ plane curve with no ${\Bbb F}_q$-linear component satisfies $N_q(C) \leq (d-1)q+1$, the only exception being the ${\Bbb F}_4$-curve $K$ with $N_4(K)=14$.
assumptions: Let $d$ be an integer with $2 \leq d \leq q+2$, and $C$ a curve of degree $d$ in ${\Bbb P}^2$ defined over ${\Bbb F}_q$ without ${\Bbb F}_q$-linear components.
conclusions: \begin{equation} N_q(C) \leq (d-1)q+1 \end{equation} except for curves over ${\Bbb F}_4$ which are projectively equivalent to the curve defined by \[ K: \ (X_0 + X_1 + X_2)^4 + (X_0X_1 + X_1X_2 +X_2X_0)^2 +X_0X_1X_2(X_0 + X_1 + X_2) =0. \]
For the exceptional curve $K$ above, $N_4(K)=14$.
nodes.origin_citation: conjectured by Sziklai 2008; proved by Homma & Kim 2009, 2010a, 2010b

nodes.name: Point-count criterion for absolute irreducibility
nodes.statement: Let $C$ be a curve over ${\Bbb F}_q$ of degree $d$ in ${\Bbb P}^2$ without ${\Bbb F}_q$-linear components. If $N_q(C) \geq (d-2)q +3$, then $C$ is absolutely irreducible.
nodes.statement_short: Enough rational points, $N_q(C) \geq (d-2)q+3$, forces a plane curve without linear components to be absolutely irreducible.
assumptions: Let $C$ be a curve over ${\Bbb F}_q$ of degree $d$ in ${\Bbb P}^2$ without ${\Bbb F}_q$-linear components.
If $N_q(C) \geq (d-2)q +3$
conclusions: then $C$ is absolutely irreducible

nodes.name: Proof of the absolute-irreducibility corollary
nodes.statement: First note that the range of $d$ is $2 \leq d \leq q+2$ by assumptions. (Step~1) Suppose $C$ is decomposed into two curves $C_1$ and $C_2$ over ${\Bbb F}_q$. For each $i =1, 2$, let $d_i$ be the degree of $C_i$. If either ``$q\neq 4$" or ``$q=4$ and none of the $C_i$'s is projectively equivalent to $K$," then \[ N_q(C) \leq N_q(C_1)+N_q(C_2) \leq ((d_1-1)q + 1) +((d_2-1)q + 1) \leq (d-2)q + 2. \] We consider the exceptional case, namely ``$q=4$ and one of the $C_i$'s is projectively equivalent to $K$ oner ${\Bbb F}_4$." Applying an ${\Bbb F}_4$-linear transformation if necessary, we may assume that $C_1=K$. Then $d=6$ and $d_2=2$, because $2 \leq d \leq 6$ and $C$ has no ${\Bbb F}_4$-linear components. Since $C_2$ is ${\Bbb F}_4$-irreducible of degree $2$, $N_4(C_2) =5$ or $1$. When $N_4(C_2) =1$, $N_4(C) \leq 14 +1 < (6-2)4 + 3.$ If $C_2$ is an absolutely irreducible conic, then ${}^{\#}(C_2 \cap \mathbb{P}^2(\mathbb{F}_2)) \leq 4$, because the maximum length of $\mathbb{F}_2$-arc is $4$. Since $K(\mathbb{F}_4) = \mathbb{P}^2(\mathbb{F}_4) \setminus \mathbb{P}^2(\mathbb{F}_2)$ (see \cite[\S 3]{hom-kim2009}), ${}^{\#}(K(\mathbb{F}_4) \cap C_2(\mathbb{F}_4))\geq 1$. Hence $N_q(C) \leq 14 + 5 -1 = (6-2)4+2.$ Therefore $C$ is irreducible over ${\Bbb F}_q$. (Step~2) Suppose that the ${\Bbb F}_q$-irreducible curve $C$ is not absolutely irreducible. Let $D$ be an irreducible component of $C$. Then $D$ is defined over an extension $\mathbb{F}_{q^t}$ of $\mathbb{F}_q$ with $t \geq 2$, and $C= D \cup D^{(q)} \cup \dots \cup D^{(q^{t-1})}$, where $D^{(q)}, \dots , D^{(q^{t-1})}$ are conjugates of $D$ over $\mathbb{F}_q$. Hence $C({\Bbb F}_q) \subset D \cap D^{(q)}$ and $\deg D = \deg D^{(q)} \leq \frac{d}{2}.$ Hence $N_q(C) \leq \left( \frac{d}{2}\right)^2$. Since $2 \leq d \leq q+2$, we have $\left( \frac{d}{2}\right)^2< (d-2)q + 3$. Indeed, consider the quadratic $P(d) = \left( \frac{d}{2}\right)^2 - (d-2)q - 3.$ Then $P(2)<0$ and $P(q+2)<0$, which implies $P(d)<0$ for any $d$ with $2 \leq d \leq q+2$. Therefore the curve $C$ is absolutely irreducible too.
nodes.statement_short: Contrapositive point counting: a reducible $C$ has too few points by the Sziklai bound (the ${\Bbb F}_4$-curve $K$ handled separately), and a non-absolutely-irreducible $C$ has $N_q(C) \leq (d/2)^2$.

nodes.name: Fix the admissible range of $d$
nodes.statement: First note that the range of $d$ is $2 \leq d \leq q+2$ by assumptions.
nodes.statement_short: Check that the hypotheses place $d$ in the range where the Sziklai bound applies.

nodes.name: Step 1: generic case of an ${\Bbb F}_q$-decomposition
nodes.statement: (Step~1) Suppose $C$ is decomposed into two curves $C_1$ and $C_2$ over ${\Bbb F}_q$. For each $i =1, 2$, let $d_i$ be the degree of $C_i$. If either ``$q\neq 4$" or ``$q=4$ and none of the $C_i$'s is projectively equivalent to $K$," then \[ N_q(C) \leq N_q(C_1)+N_q(C_2) \leq ((d_1-1)q + 1) +((d_2-1)q + 1) \leq (d-2)q + 2. \]
nodes.statement_short: Add the Sziklai bounds of the two components to get $N_q(C) \leq (d-2)q+2$.

nodes.name: Step 1: exceptional case $q=4$ with a component equivalent to $K$
nodes.statement: We consider the exceptional case, namely ``$q=4$ and one of the $C_i$'s is projectively equivalent to $K$ oner ${\Bbb F}_4$." Applying an ${\Bbb F}_4$-linear transformation if necessary, we may assume that $C_1=K$. Then $d=6$ and $d_2=2$, because $2 \leq d \leq 6$ and $C$ has no ${\Bbb F}_4$-linear components. Hence $N_q(C) \leq 14 + 5 -1 = (6-2)4+2.$ Therefore $C$ is irreducible over ${\Bbb F}_q$.
nodes.statement_short: Handle the ${\Bbb F}_4$-exception $C_1=K$ with an arc bound, concluding that $C$ is ${\Bbb F}_q$-irreducible.

nodes.name: Step 2: from ${\Bbb F}_q$-irreducible to absolutely irreducible
nodes.statement: (Step~2) Suppose that the ${\Bbb F}_q$-irreducible curve $C$ is not absolutely irreducible. Let $D$ be an irreducible component of $C$. Then $D$ is defined over an extension $\mathbb{F}_{q^t}$ of $\mathbb{F}_q$ with $t \geq 2$, and $C= D \cup D^{(q)} \cup \dots \cup D^{(q^{t-1})}$, where $D^{(q)}, \dots , D^{(q^{t-1})}$ are conjugates of $D$ over $\mathbb{F}_q$. Hence $C({\Bbb F}_q) \subset D \cap D^{(q)}$ and $\deg D = \deg D^{(q)} \leq \frac{d}{2}.$ Hence $N_q(C) \leq \left( \frac{d}{2}\right)^2$. Since $2 \leq d \leq q+2$, we have $\left( \frac{d}{2}\right)^2< (d-2)q + 3$. Indeed, consider the quadratic $P(d) = \left( \frac{d}{2}\right)^2 - (d-2)q - 3.$ Then $P(2)<0$ and $P(q+2)<0$, which implies $P(d)<0$ for any $d$ with $2 \leq d \leq q+2$. Therefore the curve $C$ is absolutely irreducible too.
nodes.statement_short: Conjugate components would confine $C({\Bbb F}_q)$ to $D \cap D^{(q)}$, giving $N_q(C) \leq (d/2)^2 < (d-2)q+3$.

nodes.name: Detour lemma for $q=4$: a cubic with 9 flexes is Hermitian
nodes.statement: Let $C$ be a plane curve of degree $3$ over $\mathbb{F}_4$ without $\mathbb{F}_4$-linear components. Suppose $N_4(C)=9$. Then $C$ is absolutely irreducible and all $\mathbb{F}_4$-points are nonsingular. In addition, suppose that all $\mathbb{F}_4$-points are flexes, i.e., $i(T_p(C).C;P) =3$ for any $P \in C(\mathbb{F}_4)$. Then $C$ is a Hermitian curve.
nodes.statement_short: An ${\Bbb F}_4$-cubic with no linear component and $9$ points is absolutely irreducible with smooth rational points, and is Hermitian once all of them are flexes.

nodes.name: Segre bound
nodes.statement: Let $d$ be an integer with $1 \leq d \leq q+1$, and $C$ be a curve of degree $d$ in ${\Bbb P}^2$ defined over ${\Bbb F}_q$, which may have ${\Bbb F}_q$-linear components. Then $N_q(C) \leq dq+1$, and equality holds if and only if $C$ is a pencil of $d$ ${\Bbb F}_q$-lines.
nodes.statement_short: Any degree-$d$ plane curve over ${\Bbb F}_q$ has $N_q(C) \leq dq+1$, with equality exactly for a pencil of $d$ ${\Bbb F}_q$-lines.
assumptions: Let $d$ be an integer with $1 \leq d \leq q+1$, and $C$ be a curve of degree $d$ in ${\Bbb P}^2$ defined over ${\Bbb F}_q$, which may have ${\Bbb F}_q$-linear components.

nodes.statement: Let $S$ be a surface of degree $d$ in ${\Bbb P}^3$ defined over ${\Bbb F}_q$ without ${\Bbb F}_q$-plane components. Then \begin{equation} N_q(S) \leq (d-1)q^2 + dq +1. \end{equation}

nodes.name: Setup: $S$ attains the elementary bound
nodes.statement: Let $d$ be an integer with $2\leq d \leq q+1$. Let $S$ be a surface of degree $d$ in ${\Bbb P}^3$ defined over ${\Bbb F}_q$ without ${\Bbb F}_q$-plane components. Furthermore we suppose that $N_q(S)$ achieves the equality in (\ref{elementary_bound}).

nodes.name: An extremal surface contains an ${\Bbb F}_q$-line
nodes.statement: The surface $S$ contains an ${\Bbb F}_q$-line.
assumptions: Let $S$ be a surface of degree $d$ in ${\Bbb P}^3$ defined over ${\Bbb F}_q$ without ${\Bbb F}_q$-plane components. Furthermore we suppose that $N_q(S)$ achieves the equality in (\ref{elementary_bound}).
conclusions: The surface $S$ contains an ${\Bbb F}_q$-line.

nodes.name: Proof that $S$ contains an ${\Bbb F}_q$-line
nodes.statement: Suppose $S$ does not contain any ${\Bbb F}_q$-lines. Let $H$ be any ${\Bbb F}_q$-plane in ${\Bbb P}^3$. Then $S\cap H$ is a plane curve of degree $d$ over ${\Bbb F}_q$ in $H = {\Bbb P}^2$, and has no ${\Bbb F}_q$-line as a component. Hence \begin{equation} N_q(S\cap H) \leq \left\{ \begin{array}{cl} (d-1)q +1 & \mbox{\rm if $(d,q) \neq (4,4)$}\\ 14 & \mbox{\rm if $(d,q) = (4,4)$} \end{array} \right. \end{equation} by Lemma~\ref{sziklai_bound}. In a term of \cite{hom2012}, defining the $s$-degree $\delta$ of $S({\Bbb F}_q)$ by \[ \delta = \max \{ N_q(S\cap H) \mid \mbox{\rm $H$ is an ${\Bbb F}_q$-plane} \}, \] we have \[ N_q(S) \leq (\delta -1)q + 1 + \left\lfloor \frac{\delta -1}{q +1} \right\rfloor \] by \cite[Proposition 2.2]{hom2012}. Hence if $(d,q) \neq (4,4)$, then \begin{eqnarray*} N_q(S) & \leq & (d-1)q^2 +1 + \left\lfloor \frac{(d -1)q}{q +1} \right\rfloor\\ &=& (d-1)q^2 +1 + \left\lfloor \frac{(d -2)(q+1)+q+2-d}{q +1} \right\rfloor\\ &=& (d-1)(q^2+1) \, {\rm ;} \end{eqnarray*} and if $(d,q) = (4,4)$, then $N_q(S) \leq 55$. In either case, $N_q(S)$ can't be $(d-1)q^2 + dq +1.$
nodes.statement_short: Contradiction: with no ${\Bbb F}_q$-line every plane section obeys the Sziklai bound, so Homma's $s$-degree bound gives $N_q(S) < (d-1)q^2+dq+1$.

nodes.name: Bound every plane section by the Sziklai bound
nodes.statement: Suppose $S$ does not contain any ${\Bbb F}_q$-lines. Let $H$ be any ${\Bbb F}_q$-plane in ${\Bbb P}^3$. Then $S\cap H$ is a plane curve of degree $d$ over ${\Bbb F}_q$ in $H = {\Bbb P}^2$, and has no ${\Bbb F}_q$-line as a component. nodes.statement_short: Assume no ${\Bbb F}_q$-line lies on $S$ and apply the Sziklai bound to each plane section.

nodes.name: Apply the $s$-degree bound
nodes.statement: In a term of \cite{hom2012}, defining the $s$-degree $\delta$ of $S({\Bbb F}_q)$ by \[ \delta = \max \{ N_q(S\cap H) \mid \mbox{\rm $H$ is an ${\Bbb F}_q$-plane} \}, \] we have \[ N_q(S) \leq (\delta -1)q + 1 + \left\lfloor \frac{\delta -1}{q +1} \right\rfloor \] by \cite[Proposition 2.2]{hom2012}.

nodes.name: planar ${\Bbb F}_q$-pencil of degree $d$ (and its vertex)
nodes.statement: Let $l_1, \dots , l_d$ be ${\Bbb F}_q$-lines in ${\Bbb P}^3$ with $d \geq 2$. The union of those $d$-lines $Z = \cup_{i=1}^d l_i$ is called a planar ${\Bbb F}_q$-pencil of degree $d$ if those $d$-lines lie on a plane simultaneously and $l_1 \cap \dots \cap l_d \neq \emptyset$. The ${\Bbb F}_q$-point $\{v_Z\} = l_1 \cap \dots \cap l_d$ is called the vertex of $Z$.
nodes.statement_short: A union of $d$ coplanar ${\Bbb F}_q$-lines with a common point; that point is the vertex.
differentia: those $d$-lines lie on a plane simultaneously

nodes.name: Notation $\check{l}({\Bbb F}_q)$
nodes.statement: For an ${\Bbb F}_q$-line $l$ of ${\Bbb P}^3$, the set of ${\Bbb F}_q$-planes containing the line $l$ is denoted by $\check{l}({\Bbb F}_q)$.

nodes.name: Plane sections through a line of $S$ are planar ${\Bbb F}_q$-pencils
nodes.statement: Let $l$ be an ${\Bbb F}_q$-line on the surface $S$. \begin{enumerate}[{\rm (i)}] \item If an ${\Bbb F}_q$-plane $H$ contains $l$, then $S\cap H$ is a planar ${\Bbb F}_q$-pencil of degree $d$. \item The map $\check{l}({\Bbb F}_q) \ni H \mapsto v_{S\cap H} \in l({\Bbb F}_q)$ is bijective. \end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: Every ${\Bbb F}_q$-plane through a line $l \subset S$ cuts $S$ in a planar pencil, and $H \mapsto v_{S \cap H}$ is a bijection onto $l({\Bbb F}_q)$.

If an ${\Bbb F}_q$-plane $H$ contains $l$

nodes.statement: {\em The verification of} ($\beta$). Let $Q_{i,j}$ be the intersection point of $l_{i,j}$ with $K$. Then the plane containing $l$ and $Q_{i,j}$ is $H_i$ and the line containing $v_i$ and $Q_{i,j}$ is $l_{i,j}$. Hence $Q_{i,j} =Q_{i',j'}$ implies $(i,j) = (i',j')$. Since \[ (S\cap K)({\Bbb F}_q) \supset \{Q_{i,j} \mid 1 \leq i \leq q+1, \, 1 \leq j \leq d-1 \} \cup \{Q\}, \] we have $N_q(S\cap K) \geq (d-1)(q+1) +1.$
nodes.statement_short: The pairwise distinct points $Q_{i,j}$ together with $Q$ give $N_q(S \cap K) \geq (d-1)(q+1)+1$.

nodes.name: A line through the vertex of a pencil section is a component of it
nodes.statement: Let $H$ be an ${\Bbb F}_q$-plane such that $S \cap H$ is a planar ${\Bbb F}_q$-pencil of degree $d$. If an ${\Bbb F}_q$-line $l \subset S$ passes through $v_{S\cap H}$, then $l$ is a component of $S \cap H$.
assumptions: Let $H$ be an ${\Bbb F}_q$-plane such that $S \cap H$ is a planar ${\Bbb F}_q$-pencil of degree $d$.
If an ${\Bbb F}_q$-line $l \subset S$ passes through $v_{S\cap H}$
conclusions: then $l$ is a component of $S \cap H$

nodes.name: Proof that such a line is a component of the section
nodes.statement: Since $d \geq 2$, there are two distinct components $l_1$ and $l_2$ of $S \cap H$. Suppose that $l$ is not contained in $H$. Then $l$ and $l_i$ span an ${\Bbb F}_q$-plane, say $H_i$. Hence $S\cap H_i$ is also a planar ${\Bbb F}_q$-pencil of degree $d$ by Lemma~\ref{planar_pencil}~(i). By the construction of $H_1$ and $H_2$, \[ v_{S \cap H_1} = l \cap l_1 = v_{S \cap H} = l \cap l_2 = v_{S \cap H_2}, \] which contradicts (ii) of Lemma~\ref{planar_pencil}. Hence $l$ is contained in $H$, and hence it is a component of $S\cap H$.
nodes.statement_short: Contradiction: if $l \not\subset H$, the two planes spanned by $l$ share a vertex, violating injectivity in the planar-pencil lemma.

nodes.name: Unique pencil plane with prescribed vertex
nodes.statement: For any ${\Bbb F}_q$-point $P$ of $S$, there is a unique ${\Bbb F}_q$-plane $H$ such that $S\cap H$ is a planar ${\Bbb F}_q$-pencil of degree $d$ with $v_{S\cap H} =P$.
nodes.statement_short: Each ${\Bbb F}_q$-point of $S$ is the vertex of exactly one pencil plane section.
assumptions: For any ${\Bbb F}_q$-point $P$ of $S$
conclusions: there is a unique ${\Bbb F}_q$-plane $H$ such that $S\cap H$ is a planar ${\Bbb F}_q$-pencil of degree $d$ with $v_{S\cap H} =P$

nodes.name: Proof of the unique-pencil-plane corollary
nodes.statement: From Lemma~\ref{contains_line} and Lemma~\ref{planar_pencil} (i), there is a line $l$ on $S$ containing $P$. Indeed the existence of an ${\Bbb F}_q$-line $l'$ on $S$ is guaranteed by Lemma~\ref{contains_line}; if the point $P$ in question lies on $l'$, there is nothing to do; when $P \not\in l'$, consider the ${\Bbb F}_q$-plane $H'$ containing $l'$ and $P$, then $S \cap H'$ is a planar ${\Bbb F}_q$-pencil by Lemma~\ref{planar_pencil} (i), which contains $P$; hence there is a line $l$ on $S$ containing $P$. Hence, by (ii) of Lemma~\ref{planar_pencil} there is a desired ${\Bbb F}_q$-plane, and such a plane is uniquely determined by $P$.
nodes.statement_short: Produce a line of $S$ through $P$, then invoke the vertex bijection for existence and uniqueness.

nodes.name: Produce an ${\Bbb F}_q$-line of $S$ through $P$
nodes.statement: From Lemma~\ref{contains_line} and Lemma~\ref{planar_pencil} (i), there is a line $l$ on $S$ containing $P$. Indeed the existence of an ${\Bbb F}_q$-line $l'$ on $S$ is guaranteed by Lemma~\ref{contains_line}; if the point $P$ in question lies on $l'$, there is nothing to do; when $P \not\in l'$, consider the ${\Bbb F}_q$-plane $H'$ containing $l'$ and $P$, then $S \cap H'$ is a planar ${\Bbb F}_q$-pencil by Lemma~\ref{planar_pencil} (i), which contains $P$; hence there is a line $l$ on $S$ containing $P$.
nodes.statement_short: Get a line through $P$ from the existence of some line $l'$ plus the pencil structure of the plane spanned by $l'$ and $P$.

nodes.name: Conclude existence and uniqueness from the vertex bijection
nodes.statement: Hence, by (ii) of Lemma~\ref{planar_pencil} there is a desired ${\Bbb F}_q$-plane, and such a plane is uniquely determined by $P$.
nodes.statement_short: The bijection $H \mapsto v_{S \cap H}$ delivers exactly one plane with vertex $P$.

nodes.name: Section 4 standing hypotheses on $q$ and $S$
nodes.statement: In this section, $q$ is assumed to be an even power of a prime number $p$ again, and $S$ is a surface in ${\Bbb P}^3$ of degree $\sqrt{q}+1$ defined over ${\Bbb F}_q$ without ${\Bbb F}_q$-plane components such that $N_q(S) = (\sqrt{q}^{3}+1)(q+1)$. Note that this number $N_q(S)$ achieves both the Weil-Deligne bound (\ref{weil_deligne}) for $n=3$ and the elementary bound (\ref{elementary_bound}).
nodes.statement_short: Section 4 hypotheses: $q$ an even power of $p$ and $S$ of degree $\sqrt q+1$ with $N_q(S)=(\sqrt q^3+1)(q+1)$, extremal for both bounds.

nodes.name: Dichotomy for plane sections: pencil or Hermitian curve
nodes.statement_short: Every ${\Bbb F}_q$-plane section of the extremal $S$ is either a planar pencil or a nonsingular Hermitian curve, and both kinds are counted exactly.
assumptions: With the above situation, let $H$ be an ${\Bbb F}_q$-plane of ${\Bbb P}^3$.
let $\nu_1$ denote the number of ${\Bbb F}_q$-planes having the property {\rm (1)} above, and $\nu_2$ the property {\rm (2)}
conclusions: $S \cap H$ is a planar ${\Bbb F}_q$-pencil of degree $\sqrt{q}+1$, or
$S \cap H$ is a nonsingular Hermitian curve of degree $\sqrt{q}+1$ over ${\Bbb F}_q$.

nodes.name: Count the pencil planes: $\nu_1 = N_q(S)$
nodes.statement: Let $\check{\Bbb P}^3({\Bbb F}_q)$ denote the set of ${\Bbb F}_q$-planes of ${\Bbb P}^3$, and $\mathcal{P}_1$ the set of ${\Bbb F}_q$-planes having the property (1). The map $\mathcal{P}_1 \ni H \mapsto v_{S \cap H} \in S({\Bbb F}_q)$ is bijective by Corollary~\ref{bijective_pencil_point}. Hence $\nu_1 = N_q(S)$.
nodes.statement_short: The vertex map is a bijection $\mathcal{P}_1 \to S({\Bbb F}_q)$, so $\nu_1 = N_q(S)$.

nodes.name: Set up the incidence correspondence $\mathcal{A}$
nodes.statement: Let $\mathcal{P}_2= \check{\Bbb P}^3({\Bbb F}_q) \setminus \mathcal{P}_1 $. Note that if $H \in \mathcal{P}_2$, then $S \cap H$ has no ${\Bbb F}_q$-liner components by Lemma~\ref{planar_pencil}~(i). Consider the correspondence \[ \mathcal{A} = \{(P, H) \mid P \in H\} \subset S({\Bbb F}_q) \times \check{\Bbb P}^3({\Bbb F}_q) \] with two projections $\pi_1: \mathcal{A} \to S({\Bbb F}_q)$ and $\pi_2: \mathcal{A} \to \check{\Bbb P}^3({\Bbb F}_q)$. Counting the cardinality of $\mathcal{A}$ by $\pi_1$, we have \[ {}^{\#}\mathcal{A} = N_q(S)\cdot(q^2+q+1). \]
nodes.statement_short: Introduce the point-plane incidence set $\mathcal{A}$ and count it by $\pi_1$.

nodes.name: Count $\mathcal{A}$ by $\pi_2$ and force equality
nodes.statement: If $H \in \mathcal{P}_1$, then $ {}^{\#}\pi_2^{-1}(H) = N_q(S \cap H) = \sqrt{q}^3+q +1, $ and if $H \in \mathcal{P}_2$, then $ {}^{\#}\pi_2^{-1}(H) = N_q(S \cap H) \leq \sqrt{q}^3 +1 $ by (\ref{sziklai_bound}). Hence, counting the cardinality of $\mathcal{A}$ by $\pi_2$, we have \begin{eqnarray*} {}^{\#}\mathcal{A} &\leq & N_q(S)\cdot (\sqrt{q}^3+q +1) + \left( \frac{q^4 -1}{q-1} -N_q(S) \right) (\sqrt{q}^3 +1)\\ &=& N_q(S)\cdot(q^2+q+1). \end{eqnarray*} Therefore, if $H \in \mathcal{P}_2$, then $N_q(S \cap H) = \sqrt{q}^3 +1$.
nodes.statement_short: The two counts of $\mathcal{A}$ coincide, so every non-pencil section attains $N_q(S \cap H) = \sqrt q^3+1$.

nodes.name: Identify the section as a Hermitian curve for $q \neq 4$
nodes.statement: Furthermore, when $H \in \mathcal{P}_2$, since $S \cap H$ has no ${\Bbb F}_q$-line as a component, $S\cap H$ is a nonsingular Hermitian curve by (\ref{hermitiancurve}) if $q \neq 4$.
nodes.statement_short: Apply the Hirschfeld-Storme-Thas-Voloch theorem to the extremal section when $q \neq 4$.

nodes.name: The case $q=4$ via flexes and the detour lemma
nodes.statement: We need a little more argument if $q=4$. We want to apply Lemma~\ref{detour}. If an $\mathbb{F}_4$-point is not a flex of $S\cap H$, i.e., $i(T_P(S\cap H). S\cap H; P)=2$, then $T_P(S\cap H)$ meets with $S\cap H$ at exactly two $\mathbb{F}_4$-points, because $\deg S\cap H=3$. Consider all $\mathbb{F}_4$-planes $\{ H_{\lambda} \}$ in $\mathbb{P}^3$ such that $ H_{\lambda} \supset T_P(S\cap H_{\lambda}). $ Let $a = {}^{\#}\{ \lambda \mid H_{\lambda} \in \mathcal{P}_1 \}$. Then ${}^{\#}\{ \lambda \mid H_{\lambda} \in \mathcal{P}_2 \}= 5-a$. Since $N_4(S \cap H_{\lambda} )$ is either $13$ or $9$, we have $ 45 = (13-2)a +(9-2)(5-a) +2$. Hence there is an $\mathbb{F}_4$-plane $ H_{\lambda} $ such that $S \cap H_{\lambda}$ is a planar $\mathbb{F}_4$-pencil of degree $3$, and the line $T_{P}(S \cap H)$ lies on $H_{\lambda}$. But it is impossible, because any $\mathbb{F}_4$-line on $H_{\lambda}$ meets with the planar pencil at either $1$, or $3$, or $5$ points.
nodes.statement_short: For $q=4$ a counting identity produces a pencil plane containing a tangent line, which is impossible, so all rational points are flexes and the detour lemma applies.

nodes.name: Last Step of the Proof of Theorem 1.2 (Main Theorem)
nodes.statement: From Proposition~\ref{sqrt_q_plus_one_case}, there is an ${\Bbb F}_q$-plane $H_{\infty} \subset {\Bbb P}^3$ such that $S \cap H_{\infty}$ is a nonsingular Hermitian curve. Choose a system of homogeneous coordinates $X_0, X_1, X_2, X_3$ of ${\Bbb P}^3$ such that \begin{enumerate}[(i)] \item $H_{\infty}$ is given by $X_0=0$; and \item the plane curve $S \cap H_{\infty}$ in $H_{\infty}={\Bbb P}^2$ is given by \[ \bar{X}_1 \bar{X}_2^{\sqrt{q}} + \bar{X}_1^{\sqrt{q}} \bar{X}_2 + \bar{X}_3^{\sqrt{q}+1} =0, \] where $\bar{X}_1, \bar{X}_2, \bar{X}_3$ are coordinates on $H_{\infty}$ induced by $X_1, X_2, X_3$ respectively. \end{enumerate} Let $P_1=(0,0,1,0)$ and $P_2=(0,1,0,0)$, both of which are points on $S \cap H_{\infty}$. For $\alpha = 1, 2$, the tangent line $L_{\alpha}$ at $P_{\alpha}$ to $S\cap H_{\infty}$ in $H_{\infty}={\Bbb P}^2$ is given by $\bar{X}_{\alpha}=0$. It is easy to see that $S \cap L_{\alpha}= \{ P_{\alpha} \}$. Hence for an ${\Bbb F}_q$-plane $H \supset L_{\alpha}$, \[ {}^{\#} \left( S({\Bbb F}_q) \cap (H \setminus L_{\alpha}) \right) = \left\{ \begin{array}{ccl} \sqrt{q}^3 + 1 -1 & & \mbox{\rm if $S\cap H$ is Hermitian}\\ \sqrt{q}^3 +q +1 -1& & \mbox{\rm if $S\cap H$ is an ${\Bbb F}_q$-pencil}. \end{array} \right. \] Counting the number $N_q(S) -1$ by using all ${\Bbb F}_q$-planes containing $L_{\alpha}$, we know that there is a unique plane $H_{\alpha, 0} \supset L_{\alpha}$ such that $S \cap H_{\alpha, 0}$ is a planar ${\Bbb F}_q$-pencil of degree $\sqrt{q}+1$; and $S \cap H_{\alpha, \lambda }$ is a nonsingular Hermitian curve for other plane $H_{\alpha, \lambda} \supset L_{\alpha}$. By changing coordinates of type \[ \left\{ \begin{array}{ccc} X_1 & \mapsto & X_1 + a X_0 \\ X_2 & \mapsto & X_2 + b X_0 \end{array} \right. \] if necessary, we may suppose that $H_{\alpha, 0}$ is defined by $X_{\alpha}=0$ for $\alpha =1$ and $2$ respectively. But the situation on $H_{\infty}$ never change. Summing up, $S$ is defined by \[ F(X_0, \dots , X_3) = X_0 f(X_0, \dots , X_3) + h(X_1, X_2, X_3) =0 \] where \[ h(X_1, X_2, X_3)= X_1 X_2^{\sqrt{q}} + X_1^{\sqrt{q}}X_2 + X_3^{\sqrt{q}+1} \] and $\deg f = \sqrt{q}$. Since $S \cap H_{1, 0} = S \cap \{ X_1 = 0 \}$ is a planar ${\Bbb F}_q$-pencil with the vertex $P_1= (0,0,1,0)$, \[ F(X_0, 0, X_2 , X_3) = X_0 f(X_0, 0, X_2 , X_3) + X_3^{\sqrt{q}+1} \] does not contain $X_2$, because this polynomial must have the form $ c \prod_j (X_0+\gamma_j X_3),$ with $c \in {\Bbb F}_q^{\ast}.$ Hence, in $F(X_0, X_1, X_2, X_3)$, any monomial containing $X_2$ also contains $X_1$. By the same argument on $S \cap H_{2, 0} =S \cap \{ X_2 = 0 \}$, any monomial containing $X_1$ also contains $X_2$. Therefore $f(X_0, X_1, X_2, X_3)$ is written as \[ f(X_0, X_1, X_2, X_3) = g_1(X_0, X_3) + g_2(X_0, \dots , X_3)X_1X_2, \] where $\deg g_1 = \sqrt{q}$ and $\deg g_2 = \sqrt{q}-2$. For the plane $H_{1, \lambda} = \{X_0 = \lambda X_1 \} \ (\lambda \in {\Bbb F}_q^{\ast}),$ since $S \cap \{X_0 = \lambda X_1 \}$ is a Hermitian curve, \begin{eqnarray} \lefteqn{ \rho F(\lambda X_1, X_1, X_2, X_3)=}\nonumber \\ && \rho \left( \lambda X_1 (g_1(\lambda X_1, X_3) + g_2(\lambda X_1, X_1, X_2, X_3)X_1 X_2) + h(X_1, X_2, X_3) \right) \end{eqnarray} is a Hermitian polynomial for some $\rho \in {\Bbb F}_q^{\ast}$. Since $X_3^{\sqrt{q}+1}$ appears only in $h(X_1, X_2, X_3)$, the constant $\rho$ must be an element of ${\Bbb F}_{\sqrt{q}}^{\ast}$. Hence (\ref{polynomialinproblem}) is a Hermitian polynomial even if $\rho =1$. Since $h$ itself Hermitian, \[ \lambda g_1(\lambda X_1, X_3)X_1 + \lambda g_2(\lambda X_1, X_1, X_2, X_3)X_1^2 X_2 \] must be Hermitian. Any monomial in $g_2(\lambda X_1, X_1, X_2, X_3)X_1^2 X_2$ never appear in $g_1(\lambda X_1, X_3)X_1$. So $g_2(\lambda X_1, X_1, X_2, X_3))X_1^2 X_2$ contains the monomials only of types $X_i^{\sqrt{q}+1}$ or $X_i^{\sqrt{q}}X_j$. Hence \[ g_2(\lambda X_1, X_1, X_2, X_3)X_1^2 X_2 = \mu X_1^{\sqrt{q}} X_2 \ (\mu \in {\Bbb F}_q). \] But the monomial $X_1X_2^{\sqrt{q}+1}$ can't appear in \[ g_1(\lambda X_1, X_3)X_1 + g_2(\lambda X_1, X_1, X_2, X_3)X_1^2 X_2. \] Hence $ g_2(\lambda X_1, X_1, X_2, X_3) =0$, that is, $X_0 - \lambda X_1$ is a factor of $g_2(X_0, X_1, X_2, X_3)$ for any $\lambda \in {\Bbb F}_q^{\ast}$. But $\deg g_2 = \sqrt{q}-2 \, (< q-1)$, it is impossible. Therefore $g_2(X_0, X_1, X_2, X_3) =0$ and $\lambda g_1(\lambda X_1, X_3)X_1 $ is Hermitian. Let \[ g_1(X_0, X_3) = \sum_{i=0}^{\sqrt{q}} a_i X_0^{i}X_3^{\sqrt{q}-i}. \] Then \[ \lambda g_1(\lambda X_1, X_3) X_1= \sum_{i=0}^{\sqrt{q}} a_i \lambda^{i+1} X_1^{i+1}X_3^{\sqrt{q}-i}, \] which is Hermitian. Hence $a_i = 0$ for $i \neq 0, \, \sqrt{q}-1, \, \sqrt{q}$; and also $a_0^{\sqrt{q}} = a_{\sqrt{q}-1}$ and $a_{\sqrt{q}} \in {\Bbb F}_{\sqrt{q}}$, that is, \[ g_1(X_0, X_3) = a_0 X_3^{\sqrt{q}} + a_0^{\sqrt{q}}X_0^{\sqrt{q}-1}X_3 + a_{\sqrt{q}}X_0^{\sqrt{q}} \ \mbox{\rm with $a_{\sqrt{q}} \in {\Bbb F}_{\sqrt{q}}$}. \] Hence \[ F(X_0, \dots , X_3) = a_0 X_0 X_3^{\sqrt{q}} + a_0^{\sqrt{q}}X_0^{\sqrt{q}}X_3 + a_{\sqrt{q}}X_0^{\sqrt{q}+1} +h(X_1, X_2, X_3), \] which is Hermitian. If $a_{\sqrt{q}} =0$, then the surface is a cone of a nonsingular Hermitian curve with vertex $(1,0,0,0)$, and then $N_q(S) = (\sqrt{q}^3 +1)q +1$, which is not the given number. So $a_{\sqrt{q}} \in {\Bbb F}_{\sqrt{q}}^{\ast}$, and hence $S$ is a nonsingular Hermitian surface.
nodes.statement_short: Normalize coordinates with one Hermitian section and two pencil planes, then force the defining form $F = X_0f + h$ to be Hermitian by monomial analysis, with $a_{\sqrt q} \neq 0$ giving nonsingularity.

nodes.name: Choose coordinates adapted to a Hermitian plane section
nodes.statement: From Proposition~\ref{sqrt_q_plus_one_case}, there is an ${\Bbb F}_q$-plane $H_{\infty} \subset {\Bbb P}^3$ such that $S \cap H_{\infty}$ is a nonsingular Hermitian curve. Choose a system of homogeneous coordinates $X_0, X_1, X_2, X_3$ of ${\Bbb P}^3$ such that \begin{enumerate}[(i)] \item $H_{\infty}$ is given by $X_0=0$; and \item the plane curve $S \cap H_{\infty}$ in $H_{\infty}={\Bbb P}^2$ is given by \[ \bar{X}_1 \bar{X}_2^{\sqrt{q}} + \bar{X}_1^{\sqrt{q}} \bar{X}_2 + \bar{X}_3^{\sqrt{q}+1} =0, \] where $\bar{X}_1, \bar{X}_2, \bar{X}_3$ are coordinates on $H_{\infty}$ induced by $X_1, X_2, X_3$ respectively. \end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: Pick a Hermitian section $S \cap H_{\infty}$ and coordinates putting it in standard form with $H_{\infty}=\{X_0=0\}$.

nodes.name: Locate the unique pencil plane through each tangent line $L_{\alpha}$
nodes.statement: Let $P_1=(0,0,1,0)$ and $P_2=(0,1,0,0)$, both of which are points on $S \cap H_{\infty}$. For $\alpha = 1, 2$, the tangent line $L_{\alpha}$ at $P_{\alpha}$ to $S\cap H_{\infty}$ in $H_{\infty}={\Bbb P}^2$ is given by $\bar{X}_{\alpha}=0$. It is easy to see that $S \cap L_{\alpha}= \{ P_{\alpha} \}$. Hence for an ${\Bbb F}_q$-plane $H \supset L_{\alpha}$, \[ {}^{\#} \left( S({\Bbb F}_q) \cap (H \setminus L_{\alpha}) \right) = \left\{ \begin{array}{ccl} \sqrt{q}^3 + 1 -1 & & \mbox{\rm if $S\cap H$ is Hermitian}\\ \sqrt{q}^3 +q +1 -1& & \mbox{\rm if $S\cap H$ is an ${\Bbb F}_q$-pencil}. \end{array} \right. \] Counting the number $N_q(S) -1$ by using all ${\Bbb F}_q$-planes containing $L_{\alpha}$, we know that there is a unique plane $H_{\alpha, 0} \supset L_{\alpha}$ such that $S \cap H_{\alpha, 0}$ is a planar ${\Bbb F}_q$-pencil of degree $\sqrt{q}+1$; and $S \cap H_{\alpha, \lambda }$ is a nonsingular Hermitian curve for other plane $H_{\alpha, \lambda} \supset L_{\alpha}$.
nodes.statement_short: Counting $N_q(S)-1$ over the planes through $L_{\alpha}$ shows exactly one of them cuts a pencil.

nodes.name: Normalize $H_{\alpha,0} = \{X_{\alpha}=0\}$
nodes.statement: By changing coordinates of type \[ \left\{ \begin{array}{ccc} X_1 & \mapsto & X_1 + a X_0 \\ X_2 & \mapsto & X_2 + b X_0 \end{array} \right. \] if necessary, we may suppose that $H_{\alpha, 0}$ is defined by $X_{\alpha}=0$ for $\alpha =1$ and $2$ respectively. But the situation on $H_{\infty}$ never change.
nodes.statement_short: A shear fixing $H_{\infty}$ moves the two pencil planes to $\{X_1=0\}$ and $\{X_2=0\}$.

nodes.name: Write $S$ as $F = X_0f + h$
nodes.statement: Summing up, $S$ is defined by \[ F(X_0, \dots , X_3) = X_0 f(X_0, \dots , X_3) + h(X_1, X_2, X_3) =0 \] where \[ h(X_1, X_2, X_3)= X_1 X_2^{\sqrt{q}} + X_1^{\sqrt{q}}X_2 + X_3^{\sqrt{q}+1} \] and $\deg f = \sqrt{q}$.
nodes.statement_short: Record the resulting shape of the defining form, $h$ being the Hermitian form of the section at infinity.

nodes.name: Monomial constraints from the two pencil sections
nodes.statement: Since $S \cap H_{1, 0} = S \cap \{ X_1 = 0 \}$ is a planar ${\Bbb F}_q$-pencil with the vertex $P_1= (0,0,1,0)$, \[ F(X_0, 0, X_2 , X_3) = X_0 f(X_0, 0, X_2 , X_3) + X_3^{\sqrt{q}+1} \] does not contain $X_2$, because this polynomial must have the form $ c \prod_j (X_0+\gamma_j X_3),$ with $c \in {\Bbb F}_q^{\ast}.$ Hence, in $F(X_0, X_1, X_2, X_3)$, any monomial containing $X_2$ also contains $X_1$. By the same argument on $S \cap H_{2, 0} =S \cap \{ X_2 = 0 \}$, any monomial containing $X_1$ also contains $X_2$.
nodes.statement_short: Because each pencil section factors into lines through its vertex, $X_1$ and $X_2$ can occur in $F$ only together.

nodes.name: Split $f$ as $g_1(X_0,X_3) + g_2X_1X_2$
nodes.statement: Therefore $f(X_0, X_1, X_2, X_3)$ is written as \[ f(X_0, X_1, X_2, X_3) = g_1(X_0, X_3) + g_2(X_0, \dots , X_3)X_1X_2, \] where $\deg g_1 = \sqrt{q}$ and $\deg g_2 = \sqrt{q}-2$.
nodes.statement_short: Deduce the two-term shape of $f$, of degrees $\sqrt q$ and $\sqrt q-2$.

nodes.name: Restrict to $H_{1,\lambda}$: the scalar $\rho$ lies in ${\Bbb F}_{\sqrt{q}}^{\ast}$
nodes.statement: For the plane $H_{1, \lambda} = \{X_0 = \lambda X_1 \} \ (\lambda \in {\Bbb F}_q^{\ast}),$ since $S \cap \{X_0 = \lambda X_1 \}$ is a Hermitian curve, \begin{eqnarray} \lefteqn{ \rho F(\lambda X_1, X_1, X_2, X_3)=}\nonumber \\ && \rho \left( \lambda X_1 (g_1(\lambda X_1, X_3) + g_2(\lambda X_1, X_1, X_2, X_3)X_1 X_2) + h(X_1, X_2, X_3) \right) \end{eqnarray} is a Hermitian polynomial for some $\rho \in {\Bbb F}_q^{\ast}$. Since $X_3^{\sqrt{q}+1}$ appears only in $h(X_1, X_2, X_3)$, the constant $\rho$ must be an element of ${\Bbb F}_{\sqrt{q}}^{\ast}$. Hence (\ref{polynomialinproblem}) is a Hermitian polynomial even if $\rho =1$.
nodes.statement_short: On each Hermitian section $\{X_0=\lambda X_1\}$ the normalizing scalar may be taken to be $1$.

nodes.name: Isolate the part that must be Hermitian
nodes.statement: Since $h$ itself Hermitian, \[ \lambda g_1(\lambda X_1, X_3)X_1 + \lambda g_2(\lambda X_1, X_1, X_2, X_3)X_1^2 X_2 \] must be Hermitian.
nodes.statement_short: Subtract the Hermitian $h$, leaving the $g_1, g_2$ contribution Hermitian.

nodes.name: Show $g_2 = 0$
nodes.statement: Any monomial in $g_2(\lambda X_1, X_1, X_2, X_3)X_1^2 X_2$ never appear in $g_1(\lambda X_1, X_3)X_1$. So $g_2(\lambda X_1, X_1, X_2, X_3))X_1^2 X_2$ contains the monomials only of types $X_i^{\sqrt{q}+1}$ or $X_i^{\sqrt{q}}X_j$. Hence \[ g_2(\lambda X_1, X_1, X_2, X_3)X_1^2 X_2 = \mu X_1^{\sqrt{q}} X_2 \ (\mu \in {\Bbb F}_q). \] But the monomial $X_1X_2^{\sqrt{q}+1}$ can't appear in \[ g_1(\lambda X_1, X_3)X_1 + g_2(\lambda X_1, X_1, X_2, X_3)X_1^2 X_2. \] Hence $ g_2(\lambda X_1, X_1, X_2, X_3) =0$, that is, $X_0 - \lambda X_1$ is a factor of $g_2(X_0, X_1, X_2, X_3)$ for any $\lambda \in {\Bbb F}_q^{\ast}$. But $\deg g_2 = \sqrt{q}-2 \, (< q-1)$, it is impossible. Therefore $g_2(X_0, X_1, X_2, X_3) =0$ and $\lambda g_1(\lambda X_1, X_3)X_1 $ is Hermitian.
nodes.statement_short: Too many linear factors would be forced on the low-degree $g_2$, so $g_2$ vanishes identically.

nodes.name: Determine the coefficients of $g_1$
nodes.statement: Let \[ g_1(X_0, X_3) = \sum_{i=0}^{\sqrt{q}} a_i X_0^{i}X_3^{\sqrt{q}-i}. \] Then \[ \lambda g_1(\lambda X_1, X_3) X_1= \sum_{i=0}^{\sqrt{q}} a_i \lambda^{i+1} X_1^{i+1}X_3^{\sqrt{q}-i}, \] which is Hermitian. Hence $a_i = 0$ for $i \neq 0, \, \sqrt{q}-1, \, \sqrt{q}$; and also $a_0^{\sqrt{q}} = a_{\sqrt{q}-1}$ and $a_{\sqrt{q}} \in {\Bbb F}_{\sqrt{q}}$, that is, \[ g_1(X_0, X_3) = a_0 X_3^{\sqrt{q}} + a_0^{\sqrt{q}}X_0^{\sqrt{q}-1}X_3 + a_{\sqrt{q}}X_0^{\sqrt{q}} \ \mbox{\rm with $a_{\sqrt{q}} \in {\Bbb F}_{\sqrt{q}}$}. \]
nodes.statement_short: Hermitian monomial types kill every coefficient of $g_1$ except $a_0$, $a_{\sqrt q-1}$, $a_{\sqrt q}$, with $a_{\sqrt q-1}=a_0^{\sqrt q}$.

nodes.name: Conclude that $S$ is a nonsingular Hermitian surface
nodes.statement: Hence \[ F(X_0, \dots , X_3) = a_0 X_0 X_3^{\sqrt{q}} + a_0^{\sqrt{q}}X_0^{\sqrt{q}}X_3 + a_{\sqrt{q}}X_0^{\sqrt{q}+1} +h(X_1, X_2, X_3), \] which is Hermitian. If $a_{\sqrt{q}} =0$, then the surface is a cone of a nonsingular Hermitian curve with vertex $(1,0,0,0)$, and then $N_q(S) = (\sqrt{q}^3 +1)q +1$, which is not the given number. So $a_{\sqrt{q}} \in {\Bbb F}_{\sqrt{q}}^{\ast}$, and hence $S$ is a nonsingular Hermitian surface.
nodes.statement_short: $F$ is Hermitian, and $a_{\sqrt q}=0$ would make $S$ a cone with the wrong point count, so $S$ is nonsingular Hermitian.

nodes.name: Ruck-Stichtenoth characterization of the Hermitian function field
nodes.statement: Let $C$ be a nonsingular curve of genus $g= \frac{1}{2}\sqrt{q}(\sqrt{q}-1)$ defined over ${\Bbb F}_q$. If $N_q(C) = \sqrt{q}^3 +1$, then the function field $\mathbb{F}_q(C)$ of $C$ coincides with that of the Hermitian curve over $\mathbb{F}_q$.
nodes.statement_short: A nonsingular curve of genus $\frac{1}{2}\sqrt q(\sqrt q-1)$ with $\sqrt q^3+1$ points has the Hermitian function field.
assumptions: Let $C$ be a nonsingular curve of genus $g= \frac{1}{2}\sqrt{q}(\sqrt{q}-1)$ defined over ${\Bbb F}_q$.
If $N_q(C) = \sqrt{q}^3 +1$
conclusions: then the function field $\mathbb{F}_q(C)$ of $C$ coincides with that of the Hermitian curve over $\mathbb{F}_q$

nodes.name: Ruck-Stichtenoth implies Hirschfeld et al. for nonsingular plane curves
nodes.statement: If one considers only nonsingular plane curves, R\"{u}ck-Stichtenoth's characterization implies Hirschfeld et al.'s, because the linear system $g_{\sqrt{q}+1}^2$ is unique if $g= \frac{1}{2}\sqrt{q}(\sqrt{q}-1) > 1$. When $q=4$, the genus in question is $1$. As was mentioned in \cite{hir-sto-tha-vol}, the plane curve $\{X_0 + \omega X_1 + \omega^2 X_2=0\}$ over $\mathbb{F}_4$ is not Hermitian, but has $9$ $\mathbb{F}_4$-points, where $\mathbb{F}_4 = \{0, 1, \omega , \omega^2\}$. However the function field of this curve over $\mathbb{F}_4$ coincides with that of the Hermitian curve over $\mathbb{F}_4$.
nodes.statement_short: For nonsingular plane curves the function-field characterization implies the point-count one; the $q=4$ genus-one case explains the exception.

nodes.name: Zeta function of an extremal curve of genus $\frac{1}{2}\sqrt{q}(\sqrt{q}-1)$
nodes.statement: Since the number $\sqrt{q}^3 +1$ achieves the Weil bound for $g= \frac{1}{2}\sqrt{q}(\sqrt{q}-1) $, the zeta function of the nonsingular curve $C$ in (A.\ref{RStheorem}) is $\frac{(1+\sqrt{q}t)^{2g}}{(1-t)(1-qt)}$.
assumptions: Since the number $\sqrt{q}^3 +1$ achieves the Weil bound for $g= \frac{1}{2}\sqrt{q}(\sqrt{q}-1) $
conclusions: the zeta function of the nonsingular curve $C$ in (A.\ref{RStheorem}) is $\frac{(1+\sqrt{q}t)^{2g}}{(1-t)(1-qt)}$

nodes.name: Ruck-Stichtenoth theorem, zeta-function form
nodes.statement: Let $C$ be a nonsingular curve of genus $g= \frac{1}{2}\sqrt{q}(\sqrt{q}-1) >1$ defined over ${\Bbb F}_q$ whose zeta function is $\frac{(1+\sqrt{q}t)^{2g}}{(1-t)(1-qt)}$. Then $C$ is the Hermitian curve.
nodes.statement_short: Restatement: a nonsingular curve of that genus with that zeta function is the Hermitian curve.
assumptions: Let $C$ be a nonsingular curve of genus $g= \frac{1}{2}\sqrt{q}(\sqrt{q}-1) >1$ defined over ${\Bbb F}_q$ whose zeta function is $\frac{(1+\sqrt{q}t)^{2g}}{(1-t)(1-qt)}$.
conclusions: Then $C$ is the Hermitian curve.

nodes.name: Zeta function of the Hermitian surface
nodes.statement: On the other hand, the number of ${\Bbb F}_q$-points of the Hermitian surface attains the Weil-Deligne bound, and its zeta function is: \begin{equation} \frac{1}{(1-t)(1-qt)^{b_2}(1-q^2t)} \ \ \ \ \ (b_2 =q\sqrt{q} -q + \sqrt{q} + 1). \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: The Hermitian surface has zeta function $1/((1-t)(1-qt)^{b_2}(1-q^2t))$ with $b_2 = q\sqrt q - q + \sqrt q + 1$.
nodes.origin_citation: classical; from the Weil-Deligne extremality of the Hermitian surface

nodes.name: Does the Hermitian zeta function characterize the Hermitian surface?
nodes.statement: It is natural to ask whether a nonsingular surface over ${\Bbb F}_q$ with the zeta function (\ref{zetaofhermitian}) is Hermitian or not.
nodes.statement_short: Is every nonsingular surface with the Hermitian zeta function Hermitian?

nodes.name: Notation $Z_X(t)$ for the zeta function of a surface
nodes.statement: From now on, when $X$ is a nonsingular surface over ${\Bbb F}_q$, $Z_X(t)$ denotes the zeta function of $X$.
differentia: when $X$ is a nonsingular surface over ${\Bbb F}_q$

nodes.name: Zeta function of a blowing-up at an ${\Bbb F}_q$-point
nodes.statement: Let $\Tilde{X}$ be a blowing-up of a nonsingular surface $X$ over ${\Bbb F}_q$ with center an ${\Bbb F}_q$-point of $X$. Then $ Z_{\Tilde{X}}(t) = Z_X(t) \frac{1}{(1-qt)}. $
assumptions: Let $\Tilde{X}$ be a blowing-up of a nonsingular surface $X$ over ${\Bbb F}_q$ with center an ${\Bbb F}_q$-point of $X$.
conclusions: Z_{\Tilde{X}}(t) = Z_X(t) \frac{1}{(1-qt)}.

nodes.name: Proof of the blowing-up zeta lemma
nodes.statement: Let $N_m(X)$ and $N_m(\Tilde{X})$ denote the number of ${\Bbb F}_{q^m}$-points of $X$ and $\Tilde{X}$ respectively. Then $N_m(\Tilde{X})= N_m(X) +q^m$. Hence \begin{align*} Z_{\Tilde{X}}(t) &= \exp \left( \sum_{m=1}^{\infty} (N_m(X) + q^m)\frac{t^m}{m} \right)\\ &= \exp \left(\sum_{m=1}^{\infty}N_m(X)\frac{t^m}{m}\right) \exp\left(\sum_{m=1}^{\infty} q^m \frac{t^m}{m} \right)\\ &= Z_X(t) \frac{1}{(1-qt)}. \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Direct computation: blowing up adds $q^m$ points over ${\Bbb F}_{q^m}$, and that factor exponentiates to $1/(1-qt)$.

nodes.name: Iterated blow-ups of ${\Bbb P}^2$ with the Hermitian zeta function
nodes.statement: Let $X_1 = {\Bbb P}^2$ over ${\Bbb F}_q$. It is obvious that $ Z_{X_1}(t) = \frac{1}{(1-t)(1-qt)(1-q^2t)}. $ Define a nonsingular surface $X_n$ over ${\Bbb F}_q$ by a blowing-up of $X_{n-1}$ with center an ${\Bbb F}_{q}$-point, successively. Then the zeta function of $X_{b_2}$ is the same as Hermitian surface's. However, if $\sqrt{q}+1 \geq 4$, the Hermitian surface of degree $\sqrt{q}+1$ is not rational. So, if $q>2^2$, then the function field of $X_{b_2}$ does not coincides with that of the Hermitian surface over ${\Bbb F}_q$.
nodes.statement_short: Blowing up ${\Bbb P}^2$ at $b_2$ rational points yields a rational surface with the Hermitian zeta function, so that zeta function does not characterize the Hermitian surface.
